### Questions

`klog` is a keystroke log of 823 people typing in English, one row per key
press. `t0` and `t1` give the moment of the press and the release, `dur` is
the hold time in between, and `dur_after` is the hold time of the next key
press. `input` is the resulting character, `null` for space and every other
key that produces no character, and `code` is the physical key. `meta`
carries three facts about each of the 823 people behind `id`: `age`, native
`lang`, and `cefr`, a proficiency band for English (`A1/A2` weakest, `C1/C2`
strongest). `t0` and `t1` are milliseconds elapsed since each person's
recording started, not wall-clock times, so they contain no year, month, or
day. Print results unless a question says otherwise.

1. Using `meta`, draw a bar plot with `.geom_bar()` showing how many people
fall in each `cefr` band.

```{python}
(
    meta
    .ggplot(aes(c.cefr))
    .geom_bar()
    .labs(title="Participants by CEFR Band", x="CEFR Band", y="Count")
)
```

2. Using `meta`, draw a histogram of `age` with `.geom_histogram(bins=30)`.

```{python}
(
    meta
    .ggplot(aes(c.age))
    .geom_histogram(bins=30)
    .labs(title="Participant Age", x="Age (years)", y="Count")
)
```

3. Using `klog`, filter to key presses with `dur` under 300 milliseconds and
draw a histogram of `dur` with `.geom_histogram(bins=60)`.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .filter(c.dur < 300)
    .ggplot(aes(c.dur))
    .geom_histogram(bins=60)
    .labs(title="Key Hold Time", x="Hold Time (ms)", y="Count")
)
```

4. The block below is given. It sorts `klog` by person and press time, then
adds three columns. `press` and `release` turn `t0` and `t1` into `Datetime`
values by casting the milliseconds to an integer and then to
`pl.Datetime("ms")`. That reads them as a Unix timestamp, so every session's
clock starts at 1970-01-01 00:00:00 instead of a real date; only the clock
time matters, and it means time elapsed since recording began. `gap` is a
`Duration`: the time between the release of the previous key and the press
of this one, computed within each person with `.over(c.id)`. The first key
of each session has no previous key, so its `gap` is `null`. Run the block
and look at the new columns.

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
klog = (
    klog
    .sort(c.id, c.t0)
    .with_columns(
        press = c.t0.cast(pl.Int64).cast(pl.Datetime("ms")),
        release = c.t1.cast(pl.Int64).cast(pl.Datetime("ms"))
    )
    .with_columns(
        gap = c.press - c.release.shift(1).over(c.id)
    )
)
klog
```

5. Filter `klog` to the first person in the table (`c.id == klog["id"][0]`),
add a `bucket` column that truncates `press` to 10-second bins with
`.dt.truncate("10s")`, group by `bucket`, count the key presses in each bin
as `n_keys`, and sort by `bucket`.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .filter(c.id == klog["id"][0])
    .with_columns(bucket = c.press.dt.truncate("10s"))
    .group_by(c.bucket)
    .agg(n_keys = pl.len())
    .sort(c.bucket)
)
```

**Answer**: This session spans 57 ten-second bins. The busiest is the second
bin (`00:00:30`) with 39 keys, and the quietest bins hold only 1 or 2.

6. Repeat question 5 and plot the result as a line, with `bucket` on the
x-axis and `n_keys` on the y-axis. Add
`.scale_x_datetime(date_labels="%M:%S")` so the axis shows minutes and
seconds instead of the 1970 date.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .filter(c.id == klog["id"][0])
    .with_columns(bucket = c.press.dt.truncate("10s"))
    .group_by(c.bucket)
    .agg(n_keys = pl.len())
    .sort(c.bucket)
    .ggplot(aes(c.bucket, c.n_keys))
    .geom_line()
    .scale_x_datetime(date_labels="%M:%S")
    .labs(title="Typing Pace of One Session", x="Time (mm:ss)", y="Keys per 10 Seconds")
)
```

7. Every session starts at the same 1970 anchor, so a bin built from all of
`klog` pools everyone's first minute together, everyone's second minute
together, and so on. Truncate `press` to 1-minute bins with
`.dt.truncate("1m")`, group by the bin, compute the number of distinct people
(`c.id.n_unique()`) and the average `dur` in each one, sort by the bin, and
print the first 15 rows.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .with_columns(bucket = c.press.dt.truncate("1m"))
    .group_by(c.bucket)
    .agg(n_people = c.id.n_unique(), avg_dur = c.dur.mean().round(1))
    .sort(c.bucket)
    .head(15)
)
```

**Answer**: 595 people have key presses in minute 0, rising to 770 in minute
3 as people who started typing later join in, then falling as people finish.
Average hold time climbs steadily, from 73.7 to 81.7 milliseconds, so people
hold keys a little longer as a session goes on.

8. A `gap` longer than 2 seconds is a real pause in typing rather than
ordinary key-to-key rhythm. Filter `klog` to rows where `gap` is greater than
`pl.duration(seconds=2)`, group by `id`, count the pauses per person as
`n_pauses`, and print the 5 people with the most.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .filter(c.gap > pl.duration(seconds=2))
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(n_pauses = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n_pauses, descending=True)
    .head(5)
)
```

**Answer**: The person with the most pauses has 176. Across everyone the
median is 41 pauses per person, so the top five are well above typical.

9. Group `klog` by `id` and compute each person's average gap in
milliseconds as `avg_gap_ms`, using `c.gap.dt.total_milliseconds().mean()`.
Then join `meta` onto the result by `id`.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(avg_gap_ms = c.gap.dt.total_milliseconds().mean())
    .join(meta, on="id")
)
```

10. Repeat question 9, then group by `cefr` and compute the number of people
and the mean of `avg_gap_ms` in each band. Sort by the average gap.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(avg_gap_ms = c.gap.dt.total_milliseconds().mean())
    .join(meta, on="id")
    .group_by(c.cefr)
    .agg(n_people = pl.len(), avg_gap_ms = c.avg_gap_ms.mean().round(1))
    .sort(c.avg_gap_ms)
)
```

**Answer**: The gap rises as the CEFR band falls: 402.1 ms for the 550
people at `C1/C2`, 585.9 ms for the 260 at `B1/B2`, and 667.4 ms for the 13
at `A1/A2`. Only 13 people sit in `A1/A2`, so that average is less reliable
than the other two.

11. Repeat question 9 and draw a scatter plot with `age` on the x-axis,
`avg_gap_ms` on the y-axis, and points colored by `cefr`.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(avg_gap_ms = c.gap.dt.total_milliseconds().mean())
    .join(meta, on="id")
    .ggplot(aes(c.age, c.avg_gap_ms, color=c.cefr))
    .geom_point()
    .labs(title="Average Gap by Age", x="Age (years)", y="Average Gap (ms)", color="CEFR Band")
)
```

**Answer**: Age shows no clear trend: most people are in their twenties and
their average gaps spread from about 100 to 1,500 ms. The `C1/C2` points sit
lower on the plot than the `B1/B2` points at every age.

12. `.rolling_mean_by()` smooths a column over a span of time instead of a
count of rows, which suits keystrokes because they are not evenly spaced.
Filter `klog` to the same person as question 5, add `gap_ms` with
`.dt.total_milliseconds()`, then add `gap_smooth`, a 15-second rolling mean of
`gap_ms` with `by=c.press`. Plot `gap_ms` as a grey line and `gap_smooth` as
a red line against `press`.

```{python}
(
    klog
    .filter(c.id == klog["id"][0])
    .with_columns(gap_ms = c.gap.dt.total_milliseconds())
    .with_columns(gap_smooth = c.gap_ms.rolling_mean_by(by=c.press, window_size="15s"))
    .ggplot(aes(c.press, c.gap_ms))
    .geom_line(color="grey")
    .geom_line(aes(y=c.gap_smooth), color="red")
    .scale_x_datetime(date_labels="%M:%S")
    .labs(title="Inter-Key Gap, Raw and 15-Second Rolling Mean", x="Press Time (mm:ss)", y="Gap (ms)")
)
```

**Answer**: The grey line jumps up and down from key to key, while the red
line stays low for most of the session and rises in a few places where the
person paused for several seconds, such as around 6:30, 8:30, and 10:00.
